¶
'''unchancy''' (un-chan′si), ''a.'' [< ''unchance'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wanchancy''.] '''1.''' Unlucky; unfortunate; ill-fated; uncanny.
{{smaller block|I cannot but think that there is no safety in having such ''unchancy'' creatures (as angels, or ghosts, or fairies, or the like) about ane.
{{right|''Scott'', Monastery.}}}}
'''2.''' Dangerous.
{{smaller block|<poem>Down the gate, in faith, they’re worse,
An’ mair ''unchancy''.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Epistle to John Kennedy.}}
I never tried him [a dragon-fly] with a hornet, they being ''unchancy'' insects to hold while one hand is otherwise engaged.
{{right|''J. G. Wood'', Out of Doors, p. 95.}}}}
'''3.''' Inconvenient; unseasonable; unsuitable.
{{smaller block|Why had his Grace come at so ''unchancy'' a moment?
{{right|''Trollope.''}}}}
[Chiefly Scotch in all uses.]

'''unchangeability''' (un-chān-jạ-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' The state or character of being unchangeable.

'''unchangeable''' (un-chān′jạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of change; immutable; not subject to variation: as, God is an ''unchangeable'' being. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.

'''unchangeableness''' (un-chān′jạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unchangeable; immutability. ''Newton.''

'''unchangeably''' (un-chān′jạ-bli), ''adv.'' So as not to suffer change; without change; immutably.

'''unchanged''' (un-chānjd′), ''a.'' Not changed or altered; unvaried.

'''unchary''' (un-chãr′i), ''a.'' Not chary; not frugal; not careful; heedless.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have said too much unto a heart of stone,
And laid mine honour too ''unchary'' out.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4. 222.}}}}

'''unchaste''' (un-chāst′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not chaste; not continent; libidinous; lewd.
{{smaller block|Kindled with ''unchaste'' desire.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5. 100.}}}}
'''2.''' Not marked by good taste.

'''unchastely''' (un-chāst′li), ''adv.'' In an unchaste manner; lewdly.

'''unchastity''' (un-chas′ti̤-ti), ''n.'' The state or character of being unchaste; incontinence; lewdness; unlawful indulgence of the sexual appetite.
{{smaller block|The time will doubtless come when the man who lays the foundation-stone of a manufacture will be able to predict with assurance in what proportion the drunkenness and the ''unchastity'' of his city will be increased by his enterprise. {{right|''Lecky'', European Morals, I. 116.}}}}

'''unche†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''inch''<sup>1</sup>.

'''uncheckable''' (un-chek′a̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not capable of being checked or hindered; that may not be stopped suddenly or forcibly. ''J. Peacock'', Sermon on Rom. ii. 4.—'''2.''' Incapable of being checked or examined.
{{smaller block|His lordship used him in his most private and ''uncheckable'' trusts. ''North'', Life of Lord Guilford, ii. 285. (''Davies.'')}}

'''unchecked''' (un-chekt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not checked; not restrained; not hindered. ''Milton'', P. L., viii. 189.—'''2†.''' Not contradicted. ''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 1. 2.

{{smaller block|If she were a long while absent, he became pettish and nervously restless, pacing the room to and fro, with the ''uncertainty'' that characterized all his movements.

{{smaller block|There is in this Iland also a mountaine, which . . . continueth alwayes burning, by ''vncessant'' belching out of flames.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 556.}}}}

'''uncessantly†''' (un-ses′ạnt-li), ''adv.'' Incessantly.
{{smaller block|Whare-fore, what may do faile vn-to hym that couaytes ''vn-cessandly'' for to lufe the name of Ihesu?
{{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 3.}}}}

'''unchain''' (un-chān′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''chain''.] To free from chains, slavery, or restraint; let loose.
{{smaller block|''Unchain'' your spirits now with spelling charms.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 31.}}}}

'''unchallengeable''' (un-chal′en-ja̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be challenged; secure.
{{smaller block|His title and his paternal fortune . . . might be rendered ''unchallengeable''.
{{right|''Scott'', St. Ronan’s Well, xxxiii. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unchallenged''' (un-chal′enjd), ''a.'' Not challenged; not objected to or called to account.

'''unchance''' (un′chȧns), ''n.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''chance''. Cf. wanchance, mischance.''] Mischance; calamity. [Scotch.]

'''unchancy''' (un-chan′si), ''a.'' [< ''unchance'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wanchancy''.] '''1.''' Unlucky; unfortunate; ill-fated; uncanny.
{{smaller block|I cannot but think that there is no safety in having such ''unchancy'' creatures (as angels, or ghosts, or fairies, or the like) about ane.
{{right|''Scott'', Monastery.}}}}
'''2.''' Dangerous.
{{smaller block|<poem>Down the gate, in faith, they’re worse,

{{right|''Burns'', Epistle to John Kennedy.}}
I never tried him [a dragon-fly] with a hornet, they being ''unchancy'' insects to hold while one hand is otherwise engaged.
{{right|''J. G. Wood'', Out of Doors, p. 95.}}}}

{{smaller block|Why had his Grace come at so ''unchancy'' a moment?
{{right|''Trollope.''}}}}
[Chiefly Scotch in all uses.]

'''unchangeability''' (un-chān-jạ-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' The state or character of being unchangeable.

'''unchangeable''' (un-chān′jạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of change; immutable; not subject to variation: as, God is an ''unchangeable'' being. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.

'''unchangeableness''' (un-chān′jạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unchangeable; immutability. ''Newton.''

'''unchangeably''' (un-chān′jạ-bli), ''adv.'' So as not to suffer change; without change; immutably.

'''unchanged''' (un-chānjd′), ''a.'' Not changed or altered; unvaried.
<poem>Naught do I see ''unchanged'' remain.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, iv. 24.}}}}

'''unchanging''' (un-chān′jing), ''a.'' Not changing; suffering no alteration; always the same.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy face is visard-like, ''unchanging.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 4. 116.}}}}

'''uncharge''' (un-chärj′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unchargen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''charge''.] '''1.''' To free from a charge, load, or cargo; unload; unburden.
{{smaller block|<poem>For-thi I conseille alle Cristene to confourmen hem to charite;
For charite with-oute chalenynge ''vnchargeth'' the soule.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xv. 338.}}}}
'''2.''' To leave free of blame or accusation; acquit of blame; acquit.
{{smaller block|<poem>Even his mother shall ''uncharge'' the practice,
And call it accident.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 7. 68.}}}}

'''uncharged''' (un-chärjd′), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Not charged; not loaded: as, the guns were ''uncharged.''—'''2.''' Unassailed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Open your ''uncharged'' ports. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., v. 4. 55.}}}}

'''unchariot''' (un-char′i-ọt), ''v. t.'' To throw out of a chariot; deprive of a chariot. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Unhorsed and ''uncharioted.'' {{right|''Pope.''}}}}

'''uncharitable''' (un-char′i-ta̤-bl), ''a.'' Not charitable; harsh; censorious; severe.
{{smaller block|<poem>Stone-hearted men, ''uncharitable'',
Passe careless by the poore.</poem>
{{right|''W. Browne'', Britannia’s Pastorals, i. 4.}}
How unequal, how ''uncharitable'' must it needs be, to impose that which his conscience cannot urge him to impose, upon him whose conscience forbids him to obey?
{{right|''Milton'', True Religion.}}}}

'''uncharitableness''' (un-char′i-tạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being uncharitable.
{{smaller block|Heaven and hell are the proper regions of mercy and ''uncharitableness.'' {{right|''Bp. Atterbury.''}}}}

'''uncharitably''' (un-char′i-tạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an uncharitable manner; without charity.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Uncharitably'' with me have you dealt.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 3. 275.}}}}

'''uncharity''' (un-char′i̤-ti), ''n.'' Want of charity; uncharitableness.
{{smaller block|Much ''uncharity'' in you. {{right|''Webster.''}}
<poem>Fought with what seem’d my own ''uncharity.''</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', Sea Dreams.}}}}

'''uncharm''' (un-chärm′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''charm.''] To release from some charm, fascination, or secret power. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor is there magic
In the person of a king that plays the tyrant
But a good sword can easily ''uncharm'' it.</poem>{{right|''Shirley'', Grateful Servant, iv. 2.}}}}

'''uncharming''' (un-chär′ming), ''a.'' Not charming; no longer able to charm. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Uncharming'' Catherine.
{{right|''Dryden'', Hind and Panther, iii. 209.}}}}

'''uncharnel''' (un-chär′nel), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''charnel.''] To remove from a tomb; disinter; exhume. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Whom would’st thou ''uncharnel?'' ''Byron'', Manfred, ii. 4.}}

'''unchartered''' (un-chär′tėrd), ''a.'' Not chartered; hence, without restriction.
{{smaller block|<poem>Me this ''unchartered'' freedom tires.</poem>{{right|''Wordsworth'', Ode to Duty.}}}}

'''unchary''' (un-chãr′i), ''a.'' Not chary; not frugal; not careful; heedless.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have said too much unto a heart of stone,
And laid mine honour too ''unchary'' out.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4. 222.}}}}

'''unchaste''' (un-chāst′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not chaste; not continent; libidinous; lewd.
{{smaller block|Kindled with ''unchaste'' desire.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5. 100.}}}}
'''2.''' Not marked by good taste.

'''unchastely''' (un-chāst′li), ''adv.'' In an unchaste manner; lewdly.

'''unchastity''' (un-chas′ti̤-ti), ''n.'' The state or character of being unchaste; incontinence; lewdness; unlawful indulgence of the sexual appetite.
{{smaller block|The time will doubtless come when the man who lays the foundation-stone of a manufacture will be able to predict with assurance in what proportion the drunkenness and the ''unchastity'' of his city will be increased by his enterprise. {{right|''Lecky'', European Morals, I. 116.}}}}

'''unche†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''inch''<sup>1</sup>.

'''uncheckable''' (un-chek′a̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not capable of being checked or hindered; that may not be stopped suddenly or forcibly. ''J. Peacock'', Sermon on Rom. ii. 4.—'''2.''' Incapable of being checked or examined.
{{smaller block|His lordship used him in his most private and ''uncheckable'' trusts. ''North'', Life of Lord Guilford, ii. 285. (''Davies.'')}}

'''unchecked''' (un-chekt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not checked; not restrained; not hindered. ''Milton'', P. L., viii. 189.—'''2†.''' Not contradicted. ''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 1. 2.

'''uncheerful''' (un-chēr′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not cheerful. {{smaller|(''a'') Sad; gloomy; melancholy.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In vain I rail at Opportunity,
At Time, at Tarquin, and ''uncheerful'' Night.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1024.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not willing; grudging: as, ''uncheerful'' service.}}
{{smaller block|Niggardly in her grants, and ''uncheerful.''
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, i. 153.}}}}

'''uncheerfulness''' (un-chēr′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' Want of cheerfulness; sadness.

'''unchild''' (un-chīld′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''child.''] '''1.''' To bereave of children; make childless.
{{smaller block|<poem>In this city he
Hath widow’d and ''unchilded'' many a one.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 6. 153.}}}}
'''2.''' To divest of the character of a child in relation to parents. [Rare in both uses.]
{{smaller block|They do justly ''unchild'' themselves that in main elections dispose of themselves without the consent of those which gave them being.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Cont., Samson’s Marriage.}}}}

'''unchildish†''' (un-chīl′dish), ''a.'' Not childish; not fit or proper for children. ''Webbe.''

'''unchivalric''' (un-shiv′al-rik), ''a.'' Unchivalrous.
{{smaller block|I distrusted her, and such vague distrust seemed an ''unchivalric'' disloyalty. {{right|''Winthrop'', Cecil Dreeme, xviii.}}}}

'''unchivalrous''' (un-shiv′al-rus), ''a.'' Not according to the rules of chivalry; wanting in chivalry or honor.
{{smaller block|Such a bad pupil, monsieur! so thankless, cold-hearted, ''unchivalrous'', unforgiving. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Villette, xxv.}}}}

'''unchristen†''' (un-kris′n), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''christen.''] '''1.''' To annul the baptism of; deprive of the rite<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
